title: US Student loan changes are a small near-term drag on spending
gist: Oxford Economics estimates the OBBBA's student loan overhaul (SAVE replaced by RAP, new borrowing caps, Grad PLUS eliminated) will cut graduate consumer spending by about $3bn a year, with ~7mn borrowers facing nearly $1,000 higher annual repayments. The drag is small and concentrated in young professionals' discretionary spending, while faster deleveraging should improve credit scores and borrowing capacity over the medium term.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics estimates that higher US student loan repayments under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act will reduce consumer spending by graduates by around $3bn a year.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A ~$3bn annual hit is macro-immaterial versus ~$20tn US consumption; not a recession catalyst.

insights.claim: The new student loan repayment formula affects about 7 million US borrowers, and the average affected borrower faces nearly a $1,000 increase in annual repayments.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Roughly $80+ per month less disposable income for affected households, a visible squeeze at the individual level.
insights.quote: We estimate the average affected borrower will face nearly a $1,000 jump in annual repayments.

insights.claim: The spending drag from US student loan changes falls disproportionately on high-income graduates and is concentrated in discretionary spending by young professionals rather than spread across the economy.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Watch discretionary categories skewed to young urban professionals (dining, travel, leisure, premium retail) for marginal softness.
insights.quote: The overall drag on consumer spending will be muted but concentrated in discretionary spending by young professionals.

insights.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act replaces the SAVE income-driven repayment plan with a new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) featuring higher repayments, delayed loan forgiveness, and measures to help lower-income borrowers pay down balances faster.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Policy shift from forgiveness-heavy relief to faster repayment raises federal cash recoveries and tightens borrower cash flow.
insights.quote: it replaces the SAVE plan with a new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), which features higher repayments, delayed loan forgiveness
insights.locator: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act

insights.claim: On the borrowing side, the OBBBA caps unsubsidized graduate and Parent PLUS federal borrowing and eliminates Grad PLUS loans entirely, with effects beginning later in 2026.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Federal pullback from graduate lending opens a gap private student lenders and refinancers may fill; also pressures graduate program pricing.
insights.quote: it caps unsubsidized graduate and subsidized Parent PLUS borrowing and eliminates Grad PLUS loans outright
insights.locator: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act

insights.claim: Faster repayments and new federal borrowing caps will shrink the outstanding stock of US student debt more quickly over the medium term.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Total student debt outstanding (~$1.7tn) could plateau or decline, a structural shift in household balance sheets.
